title: Chores as practice
hookLine: a new monk asks Joshu for the teaching and is told: wash your bowl
tomorrow: why tell the brother you cheated that his face is like God's?

lines: A NEW MONK WANTS THE REAL THING.
cards: A new arrival at a monastery, eager, maybe a little intense, goes straight to the master. He wants the real thing, and he wants it now.

In a Zen collection called the Gateless Gate, the monk says to the master Joshu: I've just entered the monastery; please teach me. Joshu asks: have you eaten your rice porridge? Yes, says the monk, I have.
Then, says Joshu, wash your bowl. And the story says that at this, the monk understood.

teach.b: Understood what? The monk thought the teaching lived somewhere other than breakfast: in a secret, a technique, a talk he hadn't heard yet. Joshu doesn't praise his zeal or hand him a reading list.
He checks whether breakfast is finished. Zen teachers read that as handing him the whole of it. Eat when you eat.

teach.h: EAT WHEN YOU EAT, WASH WHEN YOU WASH.
teach.b: Wash when it's time to wash. Don't hunt for awakening in some special place outside the day.

teach.h: HE OPENED HIS MOUTH AND SHOWED HIS HEART.
teach.b: The collection's compiler, a teacher named Mumon, adds a comment: Joshu opened his mouth and showed his heart, and if the monk didn't truly hear it, he'd mistake a bell for a jar.

Zen monasteries have a word for this side of training, samu, work practice: sweeping, cooking, weeding, washing, done as part of the path, not as a break from it. So in Zen, the chore done fully is the practice.
Not a warm-up for meditation, not a reward afterward.
The bowl, the water, your hands, nothing added. Which is harder than it sounds, because a sink is where the mind loves to wander off and argue with someone.

how: In Zen monasteries, cooking, cleaning and gardening are part of the day's training, called samu; practitioners at home try to do one chore with full attention.

o: cleaning first so you can meditate in a tidy room
a monastery rule that each monk owns just one bowl
doing a plain task fully, as the practice itself

s: in Zen, the real practice happens only on the cushion
Joshu sends the new monk to wash his bowl. the chore, done fully, is practice.
the story is a case in a Zen collection called the Gateless Gate
with a comment from its compiler, Mumon.
Joshu told the monk to meditate first, then he'd teach him
he asked if he'd eaten, then said: wash your bowl.

games.q: you've got ten minutes before a call and the sink is full. what would Joshu's answer suggest?
o: wash the dishes with your attention on the dishes, then take the call.
skip them; save your attention for the call, which matters more.
wash while rehearsing the call; doing both at once is efficient.
games.why: have you eaten? then wash your bowl. the chore done fully is the practice, not a gap before it.

practice: If there's a cup or bowl near you, hold it, and feel its weight, its rim, how it would feel under warm water. Then set it down and sit. Let the next chore you do today be only that chore, with nothing added.

wordCard.voice: Chores as practice: the bowl washed fully, not rushed to get to the real thing. Joshu's whole answer to a new monk.

orig.note: Japanese, from Zen: samu, work practice, chores done as part of training.

carryVoice: Hold this one: wash the bowl, with nothing added, the way Joshu said it. That's day 1716.
